checkpoints: The browser derives the column count by dividing the container's available width by the 220px track floor — a continuous computation as width changes, not a list of enumerated breakpoints.
`auto-fit` collapses every empty track and stretches the remaining content tracks via `1fr`, so a leftover item ends up occupying one very wide column.
`auto-fill` keeps empty tracks reserved, so the grid's column skeleton stays a fixed shape even when there are fewer items than cells.
Choose `auto-fill` when the grid must look structurally stable with a fixed column count (e.g. a thumbnail table); choose `auto-fit` when content should always expand to fill available space.
The floor is written as `min(220px, 100%)` instead of a plain `220px` so that below a 220px-wide container the track shrinks with the container instead of forcing overflow.
Grid/flex items default to `min-width: auto`, so long unbreakable content can still force a track past its `minmax` unless `min-width: 0` (or `overflow-wrap: anywhere`) is set on the item.
The observable proof of "zero breakpoints" is that `scrollWidth` never exceeds `clientWidth` at any width across the whole 320px–1920px range.
Source selection should move into markup, while only behavior gating stays in JavaScript.
`srcset`/`sizes` already let the browser pick the image by DPR and layout width, handling resolution declaratively.
`<picture>` with `<source type>` branches format, and `<source media="(prefers-reduced-data: reduce)">` branches the data-saver crop/variant in pure CSS/HTML.

`loading="lazy"` and `fetchpriority` express scheduling and priority, running at parse time before JS even loads and continuing to work if JS fails entirely — more resilient than reaching for `navigator.connection`.

What markup genuinely cannot say stays in JS: reading `effectiveType`/`saveData`/`deviceMemory`, gating a dynamic `import()` of a heavy chunk behind a capability check, or injecting a `<link rel="prefetch">` — these decide whether something loads at all, not which variant of an already-scheduled load is picked.

The signals' properties should shape how aggressively to branch: `effectiveType` is the engine's own fluctuating estimate, and `deviceMemory` is deliberately rounded into coarse buckets (0.25–8GB) to resist fingerprinting, so branching into more than two or three tiers is both unstable and a privacy smell.

Because `navigator.connection`/`navigator.deviceMemory` don't exist on Safari and Firefox, every JS branch reading them must sit behind feature-detection with a capable default, so absence degrades to the full experience rather than a broken or crippled one.
Net rule: platform-declarative for what ships, imperative JavaScript only for whether it ships.
Layout correctly reads each card's own size via `@container`, while the title's `font-size` incorrectly reads the viewport via `vw` — two different responsive mechanisms being mixed up.
`vw` is always 1% of the viewport's width, never the inline-size of any container, regardless of `container-type` on an ancestor.
Because both cards read the same viewport, they compute the identical `font-size` at any given window width, and widening the window moves both titles even though neither container changed.

Bisection: fixing the viewport and resizing one container leaves that title unchanged, while fixing both containers and resizing the viewport changes both titles — isolating the unit in the preferred term as the cause.
`clamp()` hid the bug because the `vw`-based value still lands inside the [1rem, 1.6rem] bounds at many widths, only surfacing once the two titles are compared side by side.

The fix is to swap the preferred term to `0.8rem + 2cqi`, since `cqi` is 1% of the nearest container-type ancestor's inline-size, so each card scales against its own container independent of the viewport.
Verification: after the fix, the computed `font-size` of the two titles differs at one viewport (both within 16px–25.6px), and a viewport-only resize no longer moves either title.
Two separate bugs are stacked here: the crash must be fixed first, but the wrong default-direction bug is the one a senior is expected to catch on their own.
Bug 1 (the crash): `navigator.connection` doesn't exist on Safari or Firefox since the Network Information API is Chromium-only, so reading `.effectiveType` off `undefined` throws a `TypeError`.

Because `readCapabilities()` runs at module top-level, that throw happens before `App` is even defined, so React never mounts anything — explaining why the failure is a blank page rather than a degraded one.

Adding `?.` alone isn't enough: `navigator.connection?.effectiveType` becomes `undefined` on Safari/Firefox, and `undefined !== "4g"` is `true`, so the "is it slow" check passes just because the signal is missing, not because the network is actually slow (the same happens with `deviceMemory`).

This inverts progressive enhancement — every browser lacking these APIs (a large share of real Safari/Firefox traffic) gets routed into the degraded experience by default, when optimization should reward a slow-signal's presence, not punish its absence.
The fix reads every signal behind `?.` with a capable default: `effectiveType ?? "unknown"`, `saveData ?? false`, `deviceMemory ?? 4`.

`constrained` should be derived from positive evidence of slowness only — `effectiveType` being `"2g"`/`"slow-2g"`/`"3g"`, or `saveData`/`reducedData` true — never from a signal simply being missing, so a signal-less browser falls through to the full experience by construction.

Verification: loading the app on Safari/Firefox (or a stub with `connection`/`deviceMemory` deleted) should render the full experience not blank/lite, and unit tests should assert `constrained === false` for a bare navigator stub and `constrained === true` when `effectiveType: "3g"` or `saveData: true` is injected.
Overall verdict: request changes, with exactly three findings in strict severity order (none of them tie).

Highest severity: the hero image (the LCP element) goes through the exact same lazy gate as every other image in the array, so its fetch waits for the first handleScroll run instead of starting immediately — deferring the single most important image is the opposite of the LCP goal.
Fix for the hero: pull it out of the lazy gate entirely, give it an eager src and fetchpriority="high", the same way the lesson builds a dedicated Hero component.

Next finding: the lazy implementation itself — a scroll listener that loops calling getBoundingClientRect() on every image wrapper with no throttle and no removal of already-loaded images — causes jank because scroll fires continuously and each getBoundingClientRect() forces a synchronous layout recompute on the main thread.

Fix: replace the scroll-listener loop with IntersectionObserver, which tracks intersection off the main thread and only calls back when intersection state actually changes, calling observer.disconnect() right after an image's src is assigned.

Lowest severity: the condition rect.top >= 0 && rect.bottom <= window.innerHeight is only true once an image is fully inside the viewport (zero look-ahead margin), so on a slow network the user sees a blank box/placeholder after scrolling to it.
Fix: give the observer a positive rootMargin of roughly 200px so the fetch starts before the slot enters view (too large a margin defeats the point by loading nearly every image).

Before approving, ask for evidence: a Network assertion showing a far-below-fold image URL is absent at load and appears only after scrolling near it, a priority check confirming the hero is requested at High priority from the start, and a scroll trace showing no synchronous layout read on every scroll event.

A mousemove-only reorder fails WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard): keyboard-only and screen-reader users have no way to start, move, or even perceive that a reorder is happening — no Tab to focus, no key to pick a card up, no way to hear the outcome.

dnd-kit reframes reorder as an abstract operation: each sensor (PointerSensor, KeyboardSensor) implements the same start/move/end contract for its own input device, while the sortable strategy computes positions completely independent of which sensor drove the gesture.

Both sensors hand off to the same SortableContext and the same onDragEnd calling arrayMove — the handler never branches on input type, so keyboard parity comes from registering one more sensor, not from writing a parallel reorder path.

KeyboardSensor's sortableKeyboardCoordinates translates each discrete Arrow press into the continuous coordinate delta the strategy needs: Space picks a card up (aria-pressed flips to true), Arrow moves it, Space drops it, Escape cancels the gesture.
dnd-kit's built-in live region narrates every phase — picked up / moved / dropped / cancelled — making the operation perceivable for a screen-reader user, not just operable.

One DndContext with both sensors registered gives mouse, keyboard, and assistive tech an identical reorder experience; the only mistake is forgetting to register KeyboardSensor, which is why the keyboard flow must be tested explicitly, not just eyeballed.
An overlay is paint, not semantics — Tab still walks straight through the whole page as if the modal weren't there.

Trap focus: on every Tab keydown, recompute the list of focusable elements inside the container and bend the loop at the two boundaries — on the last element with a forward Tab, preventDefault and focus the first; on the first element with Shift+Tab, focus the last; plus a safety branch pulling focus back in if it ends up outside the container.

Tell assistive tech: role="dialog" plus aria-modal="true" makes screen readers treat everything outside the dialog as inert, plus aria-labelledby pointing at the heading gives the dialog an accessible name.

Restore: save document.activeElement the moment the modal opens (usually the trigger button), focus the first element inside the dialog, and on cleanup call .focus() on that saved element — skip this and focus falls to body, so the next Tab starts over from the top of the page.
Escape is reported outward via onEscape so the parent component decides whether and how to close.
That trio — trap, aria-modal, restore — is exactly what Radix or React Aria implement under the hood.
Overall: the palette is a combobox controlling a listbox, and all three choices in the PR fight that exact pattern — none should merge as-is.

Finding 1: hijacking DOM focus (ArrowDown calling option.focus()) breaks the combobox pattern, where the input must always keep focus while the active option is only pointed at via a virtual cursor (aria-activedescendant on the input plus aria-selected on the option) — this is what lets typing and arrowing happen together and lets the screen reader announce the option via an attribute change on the focused element.
Finding 1 fix: hand-focusing the option also races cmdk's own cursor management (two owners fighting over focus), so drop the handler entirely and let cmdk own it.

Finding 2: substring-matching translatedLabel throws away fuzzy ranking (a non-contiguous query like "dshbd" should still match "Dashboard"), and because the label changes per language, filtering behaves differently per locale for the same keystrokes.
Finding 2 fix: make value a fixed, locale-independent key for ranking, with translated text living only in children.

Finding 3: registering the document keydown listener in a useEffect inside every page component means each page adds its own independent handler, so during SPA navigation without a full reload, old handlers can still be alive alongside new ones mid-transition, causing a single Cmd/Ctrl+K press to toggle the open state multiple times at once.
Finding 3 fix: mount the palette and its one listener once at the app shell (outside the router), calling event.preventDefault() to block the browser's default Ctrl+K behavior.

Acceptance proof before re-approving: role-based tests asserting aria-selected moves correctly on Arrow keys while the input stays focused throughout, a multi-route test asserting the palette toggles exactly once across page navigation, and a clean axe pass on the open dialog.
Overall: break the slowness into three separable, independent costs — network, interaction, and scale — and fix each on its own terms.

Network cost: a fetch per keystroke floods the API and races out-of-order responses; fix by debouncing the input before calling and surfacing Command.Loading while pending so the wait is announced rather than silent.

Interaction cost: replacing the whole results array on every response re-renders every row and resets aria-activedescendant, snapping the user's arrow position back to the first option and making the screen reader chatter; fix by keeping value/keys stable across updates so item identity survives, only appending items when data actually lands instead of replacing the whole array.
Scale cost: thousands of Command.Item rows in the DOM make every keystroke's filter and every scroll drag; fix by virtualizing with TanStack Virtual through cmdk's custom renderer.
The one a11y trap of virtualization: aria-activedescendant must still reference the active option even when it's scrolled out of the rendered window.

Prove each fix with a matching measurement: request count per typed word drops to roughly 1, a "press arrow then let results update" test asserts the highlighted option is unchanged, and DOM node count plus typing latency fall noticeably after virtualization.

Cursor stability is the non-negotiable part — that reset is exactly what screen-reader users experience as jitter, making it a correctness requirement of the optimization, not an accompanying nice-to-have.

Diagnose before touching code: record the Performance panel while clicking a row to reorder — the recording shows continuous per-frame Layout (reflow) events across the whole animation window, the tell that `top` and `height` are the transitioned properties, multiplied by roughly 100 rows, which floors a mid-range phone.

Fix mechanically: delete the CSS `transition: "top 300ms ease, height 300ms ease"` and the hand-assigned `tops` object, and let framer-motion's `layout` prop drive the reorder instead by wrapping each row in a `motion.div` with `layout` so FLIP does the work.

FLIP mechanism: it measures the row's box before the reorder (First), lets React apply the new order and measures the box after (Last), applies an Inverse transform so nothing visibly jumps, then Plays that transform to zero.

Why it works at the pipeline level: only `transform` animates, which the browser composites on the GPU with zero reflows, because `top`/`height` are layout properties (the most expensive step, paid every frame) while `transform` skips layout and paint entirely.

Remaining scaling limit: FLIP itself measures and writes a transform for every element carrying `layout`, so applying it to all ~100 rows on every reorder still burns real main-thread time even though it's composited, so scope `layout` to only the rows whose position actually changed rather than the full list.
Keep a `prefers-reduced-motion` gate so opted-out users get an instant reorder with no animation at all.

Validate with the same instrument that exposed the bug: re-record the Performance panel with CPU throttling on, expecting Composite/transform activity and zero per-frame Layout events, holding a steady frame rate through the reorder.

Turn the lesson into a review rule: layout is the single most expensive rendering-pipeline step and transform/opacity are the two properties that bypass it, so "never transition layout properties, use `layout`/`layoutId` instead" becomes a standing rule, not a one-off patch.
